questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Identify the effect of a clause preempting state rules on a subject
questions.stem: A planner's memo flags a federal statute that governs vehicle safety standards and states that state and local vehicle safety rules are preempted on that subject. What does that clause mean for the city's rules?

options.text: State rules survive unless they contradict the federal statute word for word
options.misconception: confuses field preemption with the conflict test

options.text: Federal law displaces state vehicle safety rules on that subject, even non-conflicting ones
No state may regulate vehicle safety at all, including matters outside the statute
options.misconception: reads the clause as a permanent blanket ban on state action

options.text: The memo is unenforceable, because a statute may not occupy an entire field
options.misconception: believes field preemption is constitutionally forbidden

questions.explanation: An express clause preempting state rules on that subject controls the field, so federal law governs even where a state rule adds to it. Treating this as conflict preemption misreads the clause.
questions.hint: Ask whether the clause names the subject itself.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Determine which local rule raises a conflict preemption question

stimulus.body: The memo compares two local rules: one banning trailers on certain streets and one requiring a permit for any trailer over 2,000 kilos. A federal rule caps highway vehicle weights and provides that no state may impose a requirement conflicting with it.

questions.stem: Which local rule does the memo suggest raises a conflict preemption problem, and why?

options.text: The street restriction, because federal law controls all vehicle use on public roads
options.misconception: assumes any federal rule displaces all local traffic rules

options.text: The permit requirement, because only weight limits are federally regulated in this area
options.misconception: thinks the federal rule's silence leaves state law untouched

options.text: The permit requirement, because it conditions hauling loads the federal cap restricts
Neither rule, because local streets are beyond the reach of any federal highway power
options.misconception: assumes local streets fall outside any federal highway power

questions.explanation: The permit requirement conditions loads that the federal cap restricts, so it invites a conflict inquiry; the street ban adds nothing federally controlled. Federal silence protects no local rule.
questions.hint: Ask which local rule touches what the federal rule limits.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: The proviso on the spending power
questions.learningObjective: State what a grant purpose condition requires of the grantee
questions.stem: The planner's memo cites the condition that federal grant money may not be used for any purpose other than the one stated in the grant. What does that condition require the city to do?

options.text: Use the grant for whatever the city judges best for the district as a whole
options.misconception: treats the condition as an advisory preference for planners

options.text: Restrict use of the grant to the stated purpose and keep records showing how it was spent
Apply the grant to any city activity that benefits the same community
options.misconception: reads the purpose limit loosely enough to cover anything

options.text: Return the grant and seek a new appropriation for the original stated purpose
options.misconception: believes grant money must be repaid if the purpose changes

questions.explanation: The condition limits federal money to the purpose Congress stated and requires the grantee to account for that use. Reading it as advisory, or as covering anything beneficial, removes the restriction.
questions.hint: Ask whether the city may substitute its own priority.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Compelling state officers to administer a programme
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a federal statute may compel state administration
questions.stem: A federal statute requires states to run a vehicle inspection programme on the federal schedule and to report results to the federal agency. Explain how that requirement may operate on the states.

answer.exemplar: The statute may require state officers to administer the programme because the duty is imposed on the states as sovereign entities rather than on private inspectors. It regulates how state officers must carry out the work, and it may be enforced by withholding federal funds, without turning every step into a direct command to private parties.

questions.explanation: A good answer distinguishes a duty addressed to state officers from a rule aimed at private parties. It should also note that conditioning federal funds is a standard enforcement device.
questions.hint: Ask whether the duty lands on the state itself.

options.misconception: treats the object limitation as a suggestion about taste

options.text: The city may keep unspent funds for the next budget year without a new act
options.misconception: assumes appropriations roll forward without a new act

options.text: The city may spend the money after the covered period ends if the work continues
options.misconception: ignores the period limit on availability

options.text: The city must spend within the stated objects and during the stated period

questions.explanation: Appropriations carry both an object limit and a period limit, so money may be used only for the named purpose and only during the covered year. Letting the city redirect or defer it contradicts both.
questions.hint: Ask what the appropriation both names and dates.

options.misconception: shifts a state obligation onto the local government

options.text: The city must comply only if it applies for a federal grant to cover the cost
options.misconception: assumes a federal duty depends on a grant application

questions.learningObjective: Determine whether a two-year plan may rest on two budget years

stimulus.body: The memo records that the federal appropriation act funds a bridge inspection programme for the first budget year and for the second, with the same amount each year. The planner asks whether the city may plan a two-year inspection contract against it.

questions.stem: What does the memo indicate about a two-year inspection contract?

options.text: It may be planned only for the second year, because the first is already spent
options.misconception: assumes the first year is consumed before the second begins

options.text: It may not be planned at all, because multi-year contracts sit outside annual appropriations
options.misconception: believes annual appropriations bar multi-year commitments

options.text: It may be planned against the appropriation, because both years are separately available
It may be planned only if the city matches funds from its own budget
options.misconception: invents a matching requirement for federal grants

questions.explanation: Because the appropriation covers both budget years, a two-year plan can rest on money available in each year. Assuming the first year is already spent misstates what the act provides.
questions.hint: Ask whether each year of the plan has money behind it.

questions.learningObjective: Distinguish authorisation from appropriation
questions.stem: The memo distinguishes a bill that authorises a transit grant programme from a law that actually provides the money for it. Which statement describes the difference correctly?

options.text: The two steps are the same, because authorising a programme and funding it are identical acts
options.misconception: conflates programme approval with funding

options.text: The authorisation approves the programme while the appropriation supplies the money
The authorisation itself provides the money, so the second step adds nothing
options.misconception: believes the first step carries the second with it

options.text: The appropriation is unnecessary, because programmes may operate once authorised
options.misconception: assumes programmes can spend without funds

questions.explanation: Authorisation creates or approves a programme and appropriation supplies the funds, so the second step is what makes spending possible. Treating the steps as one removes that constraint.
questions.hint: Ask which step makes the money available.

questions.learningObjective: Identify what a supersession clause displaces

stimulus.body: The memo describes a later federal statute covering interstate moving companies and quoting a clause that the enumerated rules on that subject supersede state regulation of moving companies. The planner notes that no state regulation of any kind was mentioned in the clause.

questions.stem: What does the clause in the memo do to state regulation of moving companies?

options.text: State rules about moving companies survive unless they contradict the federal text
options.misconception: treats supersession as a conflict-only rule

options.text: Only state rules on local moving companies survive, because the subject splits in two
options.misconception: assumes a subject split saves state rules

options.text: No state may regulate moving companies at any time, even on unrelated matters
options.misconception: reads the clause as a permanent blanket ban on state action

options.text: State regulation of moving companies on that subject is displaced, conflicting or not

questions.explanation: A clause superseding state rules on the named subject displaces the whole area of state regulation it covers, not merely conflicting rules. The other readings confuse this with a conflict test.
questions.hint: Ask whether the clause names a subject or a clash.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Assess whether a federal rule and a local rule conflict

stimulus.body: The memo compares a federal rail safety rule requiring warning signals at crossings with a local rule requiring signals to be repaired within ten days of a fault. The planner notes that both can operate on the same crossing without giving the operator contradictory instructions.

questions.stem: How does the memo describe the relationship between the federal rail rule and the local repair rule?

options.text: They can coexist, because a local timing requirement does not contradict the federal rule
The local rule is preempted, because any state rule on the same topic conflicts
options.misconception: treats the same topic as a conflict

options.text: The federal rule is invalid, because a local repair rule occupies the subject
options.misconception: assumes local rules can defeat federal safety rules

options.text: The memo shows a field conflict, because crossings are part of rail regulation
options.misconception: converts an overlap into a field preemption claim

questions.explanation: Conflict preemption requires a genuine contradiction, and a local repair deadline that can operate alongside the federal signal rule is not one. Shared subject matter is not itself a conflict.
questions.hint: Ask whether the two rules can both be obeyed.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: The proviso on the spending power
questions.learningObjective: Apply a grant purpose condition to a specific expenditure
questions.stem: A federal statute provides a grant for a pedestrian safety programme and adds that the money may not be used for administrative salaries. Explain how that condition would bear on the city's charges.

answer.exemplar: The condition would bar the city from charging its own administrative salaries to the pedestrian safety grant, because those salaries are not part of the programme the award funds, even though the work is related. It would not bar paying a contractor to install the crossing equipment that the grant was given to provide, since that is the funded purpose itself.

questions.explanation: The answer should apply the prohibition to the expenditure in the facts and distinguish it from the core funded purpose. A related activity is still outside a stated limitation.
questions.hint: Ask what the city was actually trying to charge.

options.misconception: reads a state appointment duty as a private rule

options.text: It is a suggestion, because the word requires appears inside a programme description

It applies only where a state opts in through its own legislation
options.misconception: assumes federal duties need state opt-in

questions.explanation: A statute requiring a state to appoint a coordinator and keep a register places a duty on state officers to carry out federal administration. Treating it as advisory or optional misreads the command.

options.misconception: confuses availability with actual disbursement

options.misconception: treats a federal requirement as a discretionary target

options.misconception: reads the duty as binding on local governments only

questions.learningObjective: Determine whether leftover grant money may be carried forward

stimulus.body: The memo lists two federal grants received by the city. The first covers sidewalk repair and is available for one budget year. The second covers the same kind of repair and is available for two budget years. The planner asks about the leftover first grant.

questions.stem: What does the memo imply about the leftover money from the first grant?

options.text: It cannot be rolled forward, because the first grant's period has closed
It can be rolled forward, because both grants cover the same physical work
options.misconception: treats a shared object as a shared appropriation period

options.text: It can be rolled forward, because the city may treat both grants as one fund
options.misconception: assumes the city controls the period limits of its grants

options.text: It must be repaid at once, because unused grant money is always returned
options.misconception: assumes immediate repayment rather than expiry of authority

questions.explanation: The first grant was made for one budget year, so its spending authority expired when that period ended, whatever the second grant covers. A shared purpose does not extend a period limit.

options.text: The city may always recover costs once a grant application is pending
options.misconception: invents a right to retroactive reimbursement

options.text: The city may not spend federal grant money before the money is provided
The city may treat preparatory planning work as outside the funding restriction
options.misconception: treats preparatory spending as exempt from the funding rule

options.misconception: applies the conflict test to a field clause

options.text: State rules on concession operations are displaced, whether or not they conflict
Only state rules about local concessions apply, since the subject splits by location
options.misconception: invents a geographic escape from a field clause

options.misconception: believes field preemption is never valid

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Apply conflict preemption to a local ordinance
questions.stem: A local ordinance sets a speed limit of 15 miles per hour in a residential district while a federal rule sets a different limit on a road that passes through it. Explain how a court would analyse the pair.

answer.exemplar: The local ordinance is not necessarily preempted, because conflict preemption turns on whether complying with both rules is impossible, not on whether the local rule is stricter or simply different. A court would ask whether the federal limit governs the particular road segment and whether the two requirements can be obeyed at the same time.

questions.explanation: The answer should distinguish impossibility of compliance from mere difference, and note that the federal rule's scope matters. Calling any local rule on the same road a conflict overstates the test.
questions.hint: Ask whether both rules can be obeyed together.

questions.learningObjective: Explain when parallel state and federal duties may coexist
questions.stem: A federal statute requires airlines to disclose certain cancellation fees through a national system, and a state statute requires the same airlines to post those fees on posters at airport counters. Explain the likely result.

answer.exemplar: The state poster requirement is likely not preempted, because complying with it does not obstruct the federal disclosure system and it imposes a different, additional requirement rather than contradicting the federal one. answer.exemplar: State mapping criteria within the covered area are displaced because the statute occupies the subject, and the planner should look to the federal standards for any mapping requirement in that area. options.text: Yes, because the second year's money is already appropriated and on hand

options.text: Yes, because the two years form one combined appropriation for the project
options.misconception: assumes the years merge into a single fund

options.text: Yes, because the city may reallocate across budget years at its discretion
options.misconception: invents city discretion over appropriations

options.text: No, because the appropriation is made available for the second year and the invoice falls in the first

questions.explanation: Each budget year's appropriation is available in that year, so a first-year invoice cannot be paid from second-year money. Treating the years as one fund contradicts the separate appropriations.
questions.hint: Ask which year the invoice falls in.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain what a notice of award establishes
questions.stem: The memo explains that the city received a notice of award for a park improvement grant that states both the amount and the period during which the money may be spent, while the money has not yet reached the city's account.

answer.exemplar: A signed notice of award stating an amount and a spending period reflects completed authorisation and funding, with only the transfer outstanding. The city may rely on the award and plan against it, but it may not treat the money as its own until it is actually available, and any spending before then must come from the city's own funds.

questions.explanation: The answer should recognise that authorisation and funding are complete and only the transfer is outstanding. It should also note that the city cannot spend federal money before it arrives.
questions.hint: Ask what the award letter itself states.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Identify the reach of a supersession clause
questions.stem: A statute governing national park concessions, quoted in the memo, provides that state and local requirements on concession operations are superseded by the federal scheme. Which statement about the clause's reach is right?

options.text: It reaches state requirements on that subject, whether or not any of them conflicts
It reaches only those state requirements that conflict with the federal scheme
options.misconception: applies the conflict test to a field clause

options.text: It reaches nothing at all, because a statute may not occupy a whole subject
options.misconception: believes field preemption is never valid

options.text: It reaches state requirements on every subject the city regulates
options.misconception: reads the clause as displacing all state law

questions.explanation: A clause superseding state requirements on the named subject reaches them whether or not they conflict, because the subject is occupied. Confining it to conflicts misstates it.
questions.hint: Ask what a supersession clause displaces.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Assess whether parallel reporting duties conflict

stimulus.body: The memo asks about a federal rule requiring rail operators to report derailments, and a state rule requiring the same operators to report derailments to a state board in a different form. The planner notes that the operators can keep both records without altering the federal filing.

questions.stem: What conclusion does the memo reach about the state reporting rule?

options.text: It is displaced, because the two rules address the same events
options.misconception: treats a common subject as an obstruction

options.text: It is displaced, because the federal rule occupies the field of rail safety reporting
options.misconception: assumes the federal rule is a field clause

options.text: It may stand, because requiring a second report in a different form need not obstruct the other
It prevails, because states may add reporting duties in their own form
options.misconception: assumes states may always supplement federal rules

questions.explanation: Conflict preemption asks whether the state requirement makes compliance impossible, and a parallel duty in another form may pass that test. Treating shared subject matter as obstruction misapplies it.
questions.hint: Ask whether reporting twice is impossible.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: The proviso on the spending power
questions.learningObjective: Apply a purpose limit to a professional fee
questions.stem: A federal grant for restoring a historic courthouse, described in the memo, raises the question whether the city may pay its own architect's fee from the grant. The planner must state the rule and apply it.

options.text: Yes, because professional fees are always recoverable as project costs
options.misconception: treats any project expense as an allowed cost

options.text: Only if the statute's permitted uses include such costs, because the purpose limit governs
Yes, because the architect's work is incidental to the restoration work
options.misconception: assumes incidental spending is permitted without a basis

options.text: Yes, because the city may split the fee between the grant and its own funds
options.misconception: assumes apportioning a cost cures a purpose violation

questions.explanation: The condition limits spending to the purposes the grant states, so a professional fee is permissible only if those purposes cover it. Incidence or splitting the cost does not satisfy the limitation.
questions.hint: Ask what the grant's permitted uses allow.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Purpose and period limits on appropriations
questions.learningObjective: Determine the effect of a stricter state requirement
questions.stem: The memo describes a national standard for emergency response teams and asks what a stricter state training rule would mean for the two rules.

options.text: The state requirement is invalid, because only one rule may govern response standards
options.misconception: assumes duplicate regulation is always unlawful

options.text: The state requirement is valid only if a federal agency approves it in advance
options.misconception: requires federal approval of stricter state rules

options.text: The state requirement replaces the national minimum wherever it applies
options.misconception: treats a floor as a ceiling

options.text: The state requirement operates alongside the national minimum and adds to it

questions.explanation: Stricter state requirements may coexist with a national floor because the two do not conflict. The other options assume a single-rule regime, an approval requirement, or a ceiling effect.
questions.hint: Ask whether the state rule reduces the protection required.
